data.title: Turie – Hrádek, a fortlet in the Rajecká Valley saved from a quarry
data.excerpt: A rocky hill in the narrows of the Rajecká Valley carried a small fortification that guarded the approach to the Žilina Basin from at least the Early Iron Age until the High Middle Ages. In 1949 a local teacher, Professor Hollý, halted the limestone quarrying that would otherwise have consumed the whole hill, together with a fortlet that has yielded Lusatian sherds, Roman imports and a coin of George of Poděbrady.
data.metaTitle: Turie – Hrádek: a fortlet saved from the quarry
data.metaDescription: An important fortification in the Rajecká Valley at Turie, used from the Early Iron Age to the High Middle Ages and saved from a limestone quarry in 1949.

keyFacts.label: Location
keyFacts.value: Hrádek lies in the cadastral area of the village of Turie, in the narrows of the Rajecká Valley, where it guarded the approach to the Žilina Basin.

keyFacts.label: Type of fortification
keyFacts.value: No ramparts have survived – the fortlet was evidently protected only by a timber palisade exploiting the naturally protected position with its steep slopes.

keyFacts.label: Unique find
keyFacts.value: A coin of George of Poděbrady from the second half of the 15th century is among the rarest finds from the site.

keyFacts.label: Roman import
keyFacts.value: Fragments of imported pottery from the Roman provinces were also discovered at the fortlet.

keyFacts.label: Written sources
keyFacts.value: Frankish written sources mention hillforts in this area as early as the 9th century.

keyFacts.label: Earliest written mention of the settlement
keyFacts.value: In 1416 the sources mention the lesser-noble settlement of Tres Curiae – Three Courts, later attached to the village of Turie.

keyFacts.label: Rescue of the site
keyFacts.value: In 1949 a local teacher, Professor Hollý, halted limestone extraction in the quarry that threatened to destroy the whole hill with the fortification.

keyFacts.label: Investigation of the site
keyFacts.value: In modern times Hrádek was investigated by Dr Anton Petrovský-Šichman, Ondrej Šedo and Dr Karol Pieta.

children.text: The Rajecká Valley has several important archaeological sites, but one fortification in the cadastral area of the village of Turie stands out among them. Sadly, it too did not escape an unkind turn of fate, for a limestone quarry supplying the Lietavská Lúčka cement works operated here for several years. Thanks to a local teacher, Professor Hollý, stone extraction was halted in 1949. Otherwise the entire hill, on which stands an important prehistoric fortification used in several periods, would gradually have disappeared.

The site has been known since the beginning of the 20th century. The fortification was established here as a guard post on the approach to the Žilina Basin, probably as early as the Early Iron Age, and with interruptions it was used until the High Middle Ages. Its advantageous position in the narrows of the Rajecká Valley offered good protection against an enemy. Finds of pottery fragments, iron artefacts and burnt layers of fired clay speak of intensive occupation of the site, but also of its repeated destruction. No pronounced ramparts have survived here, so it is more than likely that the fortlet was most probably protected by a timber palisade, which merely accentuated the naturally protected position with its steep slopes. The fortification was in use over a very long span of time, though certainly not continuously, since the finds recovered from this position do not confirm that so far.

The earliest finds of Lusatian culture sherds can be dated at least to the Early Iron Age, when the first fortification was probably established here. It cannot be ruled out, however, that this happened in an even earlier period – at the end of the Final Bronze Age. Another important period, when the fortlet was again used to protect the surrounding territory, is above all the 1st century BC. At that time the people of the Púchov culture lived in the valleys of northern Slovakia, and they left behind dozens of such small fortifications, but also large central hillforts. One of these fortifications stood precisely at Hrádek in Turie. The surrounding arable fields on the southern and south-eastern side of the fortification also yield intensive settlement finds – small sherds, often considerably abraded by many years of ploughing and by the weather. This too is typical of the 1st century BC, when, beside the settlement of the Púchov culture, a small fortification was built at the end of the century to protect the local population against an external enemy.

children.text: As the results of observations to date tell us, however, not one of the fortifications withstood the raid of the Germanic peoples, who arrived sometime at the beginning of the 1st century AD, or in the first two decades of the new era. At that time practically all the fortifications of the Púchov culture came to an end, including the large central hillforts such as Liptovská Mara – Havránok, Divinka – Veľký vrch, Púchov – Skalka and others. Only some of them were restored in the following period – in the Early Roman period. Among these we can again include Hrádek in Turie, which yields finds dated to the 1st–2nd centuries AD. Fragments of imported pottery from the Roman provinces were even discovered here. The restoration of the fortification evidently took place within a short span of time, because finds are once again absent from the Late Roman period (the 3rd–4th centuries AD).

Nor was this position forgotten in the 9th century AD, since it was then used once again as a fortification. At that time similar smaller fortifications also arose at other strategic positions, especially at those places where the first medieval castles were later built (Strečno, Hričov, Lednica, Vršatec). The most important hillfort, however, was once again at Divinka on Veľký vrch. It served as the central site of the whole Žilina and Bytča basins, as it had done in the preceding periods in the Final Bronze Age and at the end of the Late Iron Age. The smaller fortifications – fortlets – merely complemented the overall system of defence, which was made up of the important large hillforts. These are even mentioned in Frankish written sources of the 9th century.

At least thirty hillforts are mentioned in the territory of Great Moravia at that time, but how many of these smaller fortifications there were we can only surmise. Without detailed archaeological excavation we are unable to determine whether the fortlet at Turie also came to an end after the collapse of Great Moravia, because in the following centuries, the 10th–11th, we again have evidence of occupation here. It is therefore possible to assume that occupation of this position continued without interruption in this period as well.

An early medieval fortlet of the emerging medieval nobility may already have stood here, since occupation of the position continued in the following period as well and reached its peak in the 14th–15th centuries. This span of time has so far yielded the largest number of finds, not only pottery fragments but also iron artefacts. Besides the common, often unidentifiable fragments, these are above all iron knives, crossbow bolts, nails and mounts. The metal inventory is complemented by an iron belt buckle, and a unique find is a coin of George of Poděbrady from the second half of the 15th century. How this find reached the territory of present-day Slovakia is unknown. It may have been part of trade exchange between the local population and neighbouring villages on the eastern side of Moravia. Or it may have been booty taken by a local feudal lord who took part in a military campaign of King Matthias Corvinus. He often attacked the border regions of Moravia and even annexed this territory, as well as part of Austria, to the Kingdom of Hungary for a short time.

A third possibility is the arrival of a group of inhabitants from the territory of Moravia in the Rajecká Valley with the intention of settling permanently in this area. Along with their property they could also have brought Bohemian money. Yet another possibility remains, namely that it is a coin left here by the troops of the Bratríci (the Brethren), who moved about the territory of Slovakia for more than twenty years, including during the reigns of Matthias Corvinus and George of Poděbrady. It is therefore not improbable that the Bratríci occupied this fortlet as well and built a field camp here, from which they mounted their expeditions into the wider area. Several such fortifications of the Bratríci have been identified in the territory of Slovakia – for example Gajary in western Slovakia and Zelená hora near Hrabušice in eastern Slovakia. Here in central Slovakia we can include among them Bašta near Strečno Castle, Hradisko at Gbeľany, Posádka at Budatínska Lehota and others.

children.text: Hrádek in Turie was evidently also used for a short time at the turn of the 16th and 17th centuries, since finds of stove tiles with a yellow-green glaze, which come from a tiled stove, can be assigned to this period. These finds are not isolated here, however, because several sherds of glazed pots were found alongside them. We cannot say with certainty what the extent of this post-medieval occupation was without comprehensive archaeological excavation. Nor can it be ruled out that the seat of a local squire – a minor feudal lord – stood here, since as early as 1416 the written sources mention the lesser-noble settlement of Tres Curiae – Three Courts, which was attached to the village of Turie only in the mid-19th century.

Since the whole Rajecká Valley belonged essentially to the Lietava estate, whose main seat was at Lietava Castle, only a local steward can have resided at the fortlet in Turie. Under his supervision were the settlements in the immediate vicinity – Turie and Višňové. Moreover, at Višňové there was also a manor farm belonging to Lietava.

The fate of the fortlet in Turie was thus sealed and it remained buried for several centuries, until it began to attract attention, first from amateur searchers and collectors of antiquities and then from professional archaeologists. In modern times Hrádek was investigated by Dr Anton Petrovský-Šichman, Ondrej Šedo and Dr Karol Pieta.

Sadly, “expert” attention is also paid to this exceptional site by various treasure hunters, who have already done considerable damage to the terrain of the fortification, and only some of them have come to our museum to show off their finds as well. There really are no treasures here of the value that these “researchers” expected. What is involved here are rather “treasures” of historical value – pottery, small artefacts, the find context, which is, however, being severely destroyed by unprofessional interventions. And if it proves possible in the future to carry out archaeological excavation at Hrádek, we shall certainly be unpleasantly surprised at how much has been devastated here over the past hundred years. The quarry was stopped, but human vanity cannot be! It can overcome every obstacle and, in pursuit of a vision of “riches”, it will press on even though these and similar archaeological monuments of our distant past offer no material goods that could be turned into cash.

children.text: Sherds from broken vessels and small, often damaged fragments of iron artefacts have never yet brought anyone either fame or riches. That is why we appeal in this way to the general public not to destroy the area of the fortification, because an important monument of the earliest history of the Rajecká Valley stands here, one that several times in the distant past became a prominent landmark of its northern part. The Rajecká Valley does not abound in a wealth of such monuments. We should therefore protect even the smallest piece of evidence of our past.
